summary: Defines the application/soap+xml media type for SOAP 1.2 messages serialized as XML 1.0, so software can recognize and handle these messages properly.

plainLanguage.summary: This registers the name tag for a kind of message used by some web services so computers know how to open it.

questions: what is the soap action parameter
which media type does soap 1.2 use
subtitle: Registers application/soap+xml, the media type that labels SOAP 1.2 messages serialized as XML 1.0.

tldr.problem: SOAP 1.2 messages serialized as XML needed an official media type so software could recognize and handle them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers application/soap+xml, with an optional charset parameter and an optional action parameter that carries a URI naming the intent of the message.
tldr.outcome: SOAP 1.2 envelopes in XML 1.0 can be identified explicitly. The W3C keeps change control over the SOAP specifications.

today: RFC 3902 is an Informational registration, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Media Type Is For
sections.content:
SOAP version 1.2 is a lightweight protocol for exchanging structured information between peers in a decentralized, distributed environment. Its message construct is based on XML and can travel over a variety of underlying protocols.

This RFC defines application/soap+xml to identify SOAP 1.2 message envelopes serialized with XML 1.0. Envelopes with a different SOAP namespace version or another XML serialization MUST NOT use it.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a name tag that says 'this is a SOAP 1.2 message written in XML', and nothing else should wear that tag.

sections.title: The charset and action Parameters
sections.content:
No parameters are required. The optional charset parameter has the same meaning as for application/xml in RFC 3023.

The optional action parameter holds an absolute URI-reference, which MUST be non-empty, identifying the intent of the message. In SOAP 1.2 it plays the role the SOAPAction HTTP header field had in SOAP 1.1. There is no way to compute it from the envelope, so the value is determined out of band, and the URI is strongly RECOMMENDED to be globally unique and stable over time.

Using it is OPTIONAL. Receivers MAY use it as a hint to optimize processing but SHOULD NOT require it in order to operate.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra note on the label says what the message wants done. It is nice to have, but the receiver should still work without it.

sections.title: The Registration Template
sections.content: The registration names the type as application and the subtype as soap+xml. Encoding considerations are identical to those of application/xml, and fragment identifiers and base URI also follow RFC 3023. The published specifications are SOAP 1.2 Parts 1 and 2. Intended usage is COMMON, the Macintosh file type code is TEXT, and the contact and change controller is the World Wide Web Consortium. SOAP messages are not required or expected to be stored as files.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the form filled in for the official list of labels: name, who to ask, and which rulebook it follows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SOAP can carry application-defined data whose meaning is independent of the MIME wrapper, so the media type alone does not tell you what a message means. It is strongly RECOMMENDED to fully understand the security implications of the context in which SOAP is used. The type also shares the considerations of RFC 3023 for the +xml convention.

The action parameter is not a security mechanism and SHOULD NOT be used for authentication. If it drives decisions such as dispatch or filtering, those decisions should be confirmed by examining the SOAP envelope.
sections.plainLanguage: The label on the box does not prove the box is safe, so check what is inside before trusting it.
